grep.withFiles:
Exact lines by regex, with 3 lines of context before and 3 after each match. Regex: Rust syntax, then PCRE2; an invalid regex is searched as plain text.
Use it to narrow: exact names from what you read, all callers, limited by `path`.
For a wide search over the project use `files` with `pattern`: it names every matching file, `grep` shows 20 files per page.
`path`: files, dirs, globs or URLs joined with `;` (`src/**/*.ts;!**/*.test.ts`). One file with a line range: `src/a.ts:50-100`. Case-sensitive by default; `case: false` ignores case. A literal `\n` in the pattern matches across lines.
Files excluded by `.gitignore` are not searched unless `gitignore: false`. `node_modules` is searched only when `path` names it.
Limits: 20 files per page, in path order. 20 matches per file when several files are searched; 200 when one file is searched alone. Lines are cut at 512 bytes. Files over 4 MiB are searched in their first 4 MiB only.
The search stops at 2000 matches and the whole answer at 50 KB.
Every limit that was hit leaves a notice. Read the end of the answer:
- `Showing files 1-20 of 260. Use skip=20 ...`: more files exist. Send the next pages (`skip=20`, `skip=40`, ...) in one response, or narrow `path`. A total written as `260+` means the search stopped at 2000 matches: narrow it.
- `More than 20 matches in a.ts; ...` or `More than 200 matches; ...`: search that file alone, or by line range.
- `[Some lines truncated to 512 bytes]`, a line ending with `[col N]`: the line is cut; `read` that range.
- Any other closing notice (truncated output, skipped or oversized files, missing paths, timeout): the result is incomplete in the way the notice says. Follow it.
- No notice at all: you have every match of the files `grep` could read. Binary files give no matches. Unreadable files are skipped without a notice.
Send all independent searches in one response.
Next step: `read` the matched files whole, all in one response.

glob.withFiles:
Lists paths by mask, newest first, at most 200.
For local project files use `files`: it has no cap and prints the total.
Use `glob` for internal URLs (`skill://`, `local://*.md`, `omp://**/*.md`).
Files excluded by `.gitignore` are not listed unless `gitignore: false`.
`[200 results limit reached]`: the list is cut and the total is unknown. Switch to `files`.
The scan stops after 5 seconds: a timeout notice also means the list is incomplete, never that nothing else exists.
Send all independent `glob` calls in one response.
Next step: `read` or `grep` the paths you found, all in one response.
glob.withoutFiles:
Lists paths by mask, newest first, at most 200.
Use `glob` for internal URLs (`skill://`, `local://*.md`, `omp://**/*.md`).
Files excluded by `.gitignore` are not listed unless `gitignore: false`.
No paging and no total. "[200 results limit reached]": the list is cut. Split the mask by directory or extension and send the parts in one response.
The scan stops after 5 seconds: a timeout notice also means the list is incomplete, never that nothing else exists.
Send all independent `glob` calls in one response.
Next step: `read` or `grep` the paths you found, all in one response.

read:
Reads a file. Default: the whole file, bare path.
Read every file you need in one response: independent reads run in parallel.
One call returns at most 3000 lines and 100 KB.
- `[Showing lines 1-3000 of 9000. Use :3001 to continue]`: cut by lines. Read the rest in one response: `path:3001-6000` and `path:6001-9000`.
- `[Showing lines 1-169 of 300 (100.0KB limit). Use :170 to continue]`: cut by size. Continue from the named line; split the rest into ranges of about the shown size, all in one response.
A range read ends with `[Showing lines A-B of N. Use :B+1 to continue]`: it marks the end of your range, not a cut. Continue only if you need more lines.
Any other closing notice names what was cut and how to continue: follow it.
Never treat a cut file or a range as the whole file.
A bare path with no cut marker is the whole file; a range is a part of the file unless its shown lines cover the file.
A whole-file read ends with `[whole file: N lines]`: every line is there.
Ranges go in `path`: `a.ts:120-180`, `a.ts:-60` (last 60), `a.ts:5-16,960-973`.
Web pages: at most 300 lines and 50 KB per call.
Sources:
- Directory: complete root; child listings cap at 12 (`… N more`), read child; page via :N-M/:-N.
- SQLite: file.db tables; :table schema/rows; :table:key by primary key; ?limit=, ?where=, ?q=SELECT.
- Archives: ZIP/JAR/APK/WHL, compressed TAR, RAR/7z/ISO/CAB/DEB/RPM/CPIO/AR/LZH/ARJ/ASAR, compressed streams; member via archive.ext:member/path.
- JSON/JSONL/NDJSON: file.json?q=<jq filter>; &raw=true unquoted strings, &compact=true one-line values, &offset=&limit= page array elements or result values; `&` inside the filter → %26. The output is text, not one JSON document.
- PDF/documents: extracted text; notebooks: editable cells; images: decoded inline. URLs: reader text/markdown, :raw original HTML; bare host:port needs trailing slash.
Next step: follow imports and calls to the next files and read them in one response; `grep` exact names; then `edit`.

bash.withFiles:
Terminal only: git, tests, builds, package managers, running programs.
Not for reading, listing or searching files. `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `ls`, `find`, `grep`, `rg`, `sed -n` are blocked: use `read`, `files`, `grep`.
`cwd` sets the directory; never `cd`. Independent commands are separate calls in one response: they run in parallel. Dependent commands are joined with `&&`.
Output over 50 KB keeps its head and tail, the middle is cut: `[Showing lines 1-N and M-K of K; ... middle lines elided. Read artifact://0 for full output]`. `read` the artifact.
Next step: after `edit`, run the narrow check (a test, a build, `git diff`).
Persistent shell: one fact command/pipeline; dependencies use `&&`.
Scripts/heredocs/`$(…)`/complex pipelines → `eval`.
`cwd`, not `cd`; `pty` only interactive.
Internal URIs work as paths for builtins/coreutils, redirects, globs.
`async` defers finite results but keeps the deadline (default 300s); `timeout: 0` for watchers and long jobs.
No `head`/`tail`/redirection; output trunc by default, full result at `artifact://<id>`.
Long-lived services: unique name; ready requires name; no async/timeout; pty defaults true. ready needs log regex or port (both if given); host defaults 127.0.0.1, ready.timeout 30s.
Non-`pty` calls still running after 60s (or 1s before `timeout`, if sooner) usually move to background job `bg_N` and keep running to `timeout` (not when the client terminal runs the command or the job cap is reached); the result arrives automatically as a follow-up message. NEVER poll.

edit:
Applies a patch. One call carries every ready change: any number of files, with `Add File`, `Update File`, `Delete File`, `Move to` sections.
Read a file before you change it. Then send all edits of the task in ONE patch, not one call per file: `edit` calls run one after another.
Files of a patch apply independently. A file with a section that does not match is skipped and not changed; every other file is written. The answer names each skipped file with the reason: re-read it and resend only that file.
Next step: a narrow check through `bash`.

`apply_patch`: stripped-down, file-oriented diff; easy to parse, safe to apply.

Envelope:
```
*** Begin Patch
[ one or more file sections ]
*** End Patch
```
Contains file operations. Each MUST have an action header:

`*** Add File: <path>`: create file; every following line `+` (initial contents).

`*** Delete File: <path>`: remove existing file; nothing follows.

`*** Update File: <path>`: patch existing file in place; optional immediate `*** Move to: <new path>` renames it; then one or more `@@` hunks (optional hunk header). Omit hunks only for a content-preserving move. Hunk lines start with space, `-`, or `+`.

Old/context lines must match complete file lines, allowing only whitespace and Unicode punctuation normalization, not substrings or similar text.

Context: default 3 code lines immediately before and after each change. Changes within 3 lines: do NOT duplicate first change's context-after lines as second change's context-before lines. If 3 lines do not uniquely identify code in the file, use `@@` with its class/function; if one `@@` plus 3 context lines still cannot uniquely identify repeated code in a class/function, use multiple `@@` lines to reach it:
```
@@ class BaseClass
[3 lines of pre-context]
- [old_code]
+ [new_code]
[3 lines of post-context]
```
```
@@ class BaseClass
@@ 	 def method():
[3 lines of pre-context]
- [old_code]
+ [new_code]
[3 lines of post-context]
```

Grammar:
```
Patch := Begin { FileOp } End
Begin := "*** Begin Patch" NEWLINE
End := "*** End Patch" NEWLINE
FileOp := AddFile | DeleteFile | UpdateFile
AddFile := "*** Add File: " path NEWLINE { "+" line NEWLINE }
DeleteFile := "*** Delete File: " path NEWLINE
UpdateFile := "*** Update File: " path NEWLINE [ MoveTo ] { Hunk }
MoveTo := "*** Move to: " newPath NEWLINE
Hunk := "@@" [ header ] NEWLINE { HunkLine } [ "*** End of File" NEWLINE ]
HunkLine := (" " | "-" | "+") text NEWLINE
```

Full patches may combine operations:
```
*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: hello.txt
+Hello world
*** Update File: src/app.py
*** Move to: src/main.py
@@ def greet():
-print("Hi")
+print("Hello, world!")
*** Delete File: obsolete.txt
*** End Patch
```

MUST use Add/Delete/Update header; new-file lines MUST start `+`; file references relative, NEVER absolute.

<examples>
# Apply a combined patch file
<example i="…">

*** Add File: hello.txt
+Hello world

@@ def greet():

write:
Creates one file or replaces it fully.
Several new files: send all `write` calls in one response (they run one after another), or use `Add File` sections in one `edit` patch.
Replacing an existing file: read it whole first. `write` replaces the whole file: every line you did not read is lost.
A small change in an existing file: `edit`.
Next step: a narrow check through `bash`.

skipped.head: Partial patch: the files below did not match and are NOT changed. Their sections were removed from this call automatically before it ran. The result of the remaining files follows this note.
skipped.tail: Re-read each skipped file, fix its section and send it again. Do not resend files that are already written.
